title: OpenAI Agrees Pentagon AI Deal With Key Ethical Safeguards

WASHINGTON (Azat TV) – OpenAI announced Friday it has struck a deal with the U.S. Department of Defense to deploy its artificial intelligence models on the Pentagon’s classified network, incorporating crucial “safeguards” against domestic mass surveillance and fully autonomous weapons systems. This agreement comes just hours after President Donald Trump’s administration blacklisted AI rival Anthropic for refusing unconditional military use of its own Claude models, creating a stark contrast in the government’s engagement with leading AI firms on ethical military applications.Related ArticlesOmani FM Revealed US-Iran Deal Was Near Before Trump’s StrikesMacron Calls US-Israel Attack on Iran ‘Dangerous’ Amid EscalationLawmakers Demand Vote After Trump Launches Iran Operation The deal, confirmed by OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, includes specific prohibitions that mirror the “red lines” Anthropic had insisted upon. Altman stated on X that two of OpenAI’s “most important safety principles are prohibitions on domestic mass surveillance and human responsibility for the use of force, including for autonomous weapon systems,” adding that these principles were integrated “into our agreement.” The Department of Defense did not immediately comment on the specifics of the arrangement. OpenAI’s Safeguarded Pentagon Agreement OpenAI’s agreement with the Pentagon marks a significant moment in the evolving relationship between the U.S. military and cutting-edge artificial intelligence developers. The company’s models will be integrated into the defense agency’s classified network, with the stipulation that their use will adhere to strict ethical guidelines. These guidelines explicitly forbid their deployment for mass surveillance of American citizens and ensure that human oversight remains central to any decisions involving the use of force, particularly concerning autonomous weapon systems. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman had reportedly communicated to employees that he was seeking an agreement with terms similar to those Anthropic had proposed, underscoring a shared industry concern for responsible AI deployment. Anthropic’s Blacklisting and Government Pressure The backdrop to OpenAI’s deal is the dramatic fallout between the Trump administration and Anthropic. Just hours before OpenAI’s announcement, President Trump issued a directive ordering all federal agencies to immediately cease using Anthropic’s technology. This executive action followed Anthropic’s steadfast refusal to grant the Pentagon unconditional access to its Claude models, citing ethical concerns over mass surveillance and fully autonomous weapons. The administration had responded aggressively, threatening Anthropic with compulsion under the Cold War-era Defense Production Act and the designation of a “supply chain risk” – a label typically reserved for companies from adversary nations. U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth publicly condemned Anthropic, calling its stance a “master class in arrogance and betrayal.” Anthropic, a San Francisco-based AI startup, vowed to challenge any such designation in court, reiterating its commitment to its safety principles. Industry Backlash and Unanswered Questions The conflict between the U.S. government and Anthropic had drawn widespread concern within the tech industry. Hundreds of employees from major AI firms, including Google DeepMind and OpenAI, signed an open letter titled “We Will Not Be Divided,” urging their companies to stand in solidarity with Anthropic’s ethical demands.
